Ask Day of Week 今天星期几？; Jīntiān xīngqī jǐ?; What day of the week is it? 今天星期二。; Jīntiān xīngqī'èr.; Today is Tuesday. Ask Birthday 你的生日是几月几号？; Nǐ de shēngrì shì jǐ yuè jǐ hào?; When is your birthday? 我的生日是三月十二号。; Wǒ de shēngrì shì sān yuè shí'èr hào.; My birthday is March 12th.

💡 Measure Word Quick Guide: 个 (gè): The universal, everyday measure word for individual people. 位 (wèi): A respectful / polite measure word (敬词) used for elders, respected figures, or formal contexts (e.g., 一位母亲, 一位爷爷). Not typically used for children or younger siblings. 对 (duì): "A pair / couple", used for paired relationships like parents (一对父母) or married couples (一对夫妻). 群 (qún): "A group", used for multiple children (一群孩子). 口 (kǒu): Specifically used when counting the total number of members in a household (e.g., 一家五口人 = "a family of five"). Category Standard / Formal Term Casual / Regional Form Measure Words Example with Measure Word Notes Immediate Family 爸爸; bàba; Father / Dad 爸; bà; Dad 个 (gè), 位 (wèi) 一个好爸爸 (yí gè hǎo bàba — a good dad) 一位伟大的父亲 (yí wèi wěidà de fùqīn — a great father) 位 (wèi) adds respect or formality. Immediate Family 妈妈; māma; Mother / Mom 妈; mā; Mom 个 (gè), 位 (wèi) 一个温柔的妈妈 (yí gè wēnróu de māma — a gentle mom) 一位慈爱的母亲 (yí wèi cí'ài de mǔqīn — a loving mother) Formal variant: 母亲; mǔqīn. Immediate Family 哥哥; gēge; Older br /other 哥; gē; Br /o 个 (gè) 一个亲哥哥 (yí gè qīn gēge — an older biological br /other) 两个哥哥 (liǎng gè gēge — two older br /others) 位 is generally not used for siblings. Immediate Family 弟弟; dìdi; Younger br /other 弟; dì; Younger br /other 个 (gè) 一个调皮的弟弟 (yí gè tiáopí de dìdi — a mischievous little br /other) — Immediate Family 姐姐; jiějie; Older sister 姐; jiě; Older sister 个 (gè) 一个漂亮的姐姐 (yí gè piàoliang de jiějie — a pretty older sister) — Immediate Family 妹妹; mèimei; Younger sister 妹; mèi; Younger sister 个 (gè) 一个可爱的妹妹 (yí gè kě'ài de mèimei — a cute little sister) — Immediate Family 儿子; érzi; Son — 个 (gè), 名 (míng) 一个听话的儿子 (yí gè tīnghuà de érzi — an obedient son) 一名独生儿子 (yì míng dúshēng érzi — an only son [formal]) 名 (míng) is used in formal/official registers. Immediate Family 女儿; nǚ'ér; Daughter — 个 (gè), 名 (míng) 一个乖女儿 (yí gè guāi nǚ'ér — a good/sweet daughter) 两名女儿 (liǎng míng nǚ'ér — two daughters [formal]) Literally "female child". Immediate Family 丈夫; zhàngfu; Husband 老公; lǎogōng; Husband (casual) 个 (gè), 位 (wèi) 一位体贴的丈夫 (yí wèi tǐtiē de zhàngfu — a considerate husband) 一个好老公 (yí gè hǎo lǎogōng — a great hubby) 位 (wèi) is natural with 丈夫; 个 (gè) is used with 老公. Immediate Family 妻子; qīzi; Wife 老婆; lǎopó; Wife (casual) 个 (gè), 位 (wèi) 一位贤惠的妻子 (yí wèi xiánhuì de qīzi — a virtuous wife) 一个漂亮老婆 (yí gè piàoliang lǎopó — a pretty wife) 位 (wèi) is natural with 妻子; 个 (gè) is used with 老婆. Collective Terms 父母; fùmǔ; Parents 爸妈 (bàmā) 对 (duì), 位 (wèi) 一对开明的父母 (yí duì kāimíng de fùmǔ — an open-minded set of parents) 两位父母 (liǎng wèi fùmǔ — both parents) 对 = pair/couple; 两位 = both individuals politely. Collective Terms 兄弟姐妹; xiōngdì jiěmèi; Siblings — 个 (gè) 四个兄弟姐妹 (sì gè xiōngdì jiěmèi — four siblings) 没有兄弟姐妹 (méiyǒu xiōngdì jiěmèi — have no siblings) Counted with standard 个 (gè). Collective Terms 孩子; háizi; Child / Children 娃 / 娃儿 (wá / wár) 个 (gè), 群 (qún), 名 (míng) 三个孩子 (sān gè háizi — three kids) 一群快乐的孩子 (yì qún kuàilè de háizi — a group of happy kids) 群 (qún) = group; 名 (míng) for official forms. Paternal Grandparents 爷爷; yéye; Grandfather (paternal) — 个 (gè), 位 (wèi) 一位和蔼的爷爷 (yí wèi hé'ǎi de yéye — an amiable grandfather) Father's father; 位 (wèi) conveys elder respect. Paternal Grandparents 奶奶; nǎinai; Grandmother (paternal) — 个 (gè), 位 (wèi) 一位慈祥的奶奶 (yí wèi cíxiáng de nǎinai — a kindly grandmother) Father's mother. Maternal Grandparents 外公; wàigōng; Grandfather (maternal) 老爷; lǎoye; Grandfather (Northern) 个 (gè), 位 (wèi) 一位健康的外公 (yí wèi jiànkāng de wàigōng — a healthy grandfather) 一个开朗的老爷 (yí gè kāilǎng de lǎoye — a cheerful grandpa) Mother's father; 外 (wài) literally means "outside/external". Maternal Grandparents 外婆; wàipó; Grandmother (maternal) 姥姥; lǎolao; Grandmother (Northern) 个 (gè), 位 (wèi) 一位勤劳的外婆 (yí wèi qínláo de wàipó — a hardworking grandmother) 一个亲切的姥姥 (yí gè qīnqiè de lǎolao — a warm grandma) Mother's mother.

⚠️ The Golden Word Order for Titles: In English, titles precede the surname ("Mr. Wang", "Teacher Zhang"). In Mandarin, the surname ALWAYS comes first: [Surname] + [Title] ➔ 王先生; Wáng xiānsheng; Mr. Wang, 张老师; Zhāng lǎoshī; Teacher Zhang, 李经理; Lǐ jīnglǐ; Manager Li 💡 Measure Word Guide for Titles: 位 (wèi): The primary polite / respectful measure word (敬词) for guests, experts, professionals, and elders (一位教授, 一位领导). 名 (míng): Formal and objective, common in news, administrative, legal, and academic registers (一名律师, 一名警察). 个 (gè): Universal and casual; acceptable in everyday informal conversation (一个服务员, 一个同事). Domain & Level Standard Title / Term Direct Address / Formula Measure Words Example with Measure Word Social Context & Usage Notes Honorific / Gender HSK 1 先生; xiānsheng; Mr. / Sir / Gentleman Surname + 先生 (e.g., 王先生) 位 (wèi), 个 (gè) 一位有礼貌的先生 (yí wèi yǒu lǐmào de xiānsheng — a polite gentleman) Universal respectful address for adult men in business, services, and formal settings. Honorific / Gender HSK 4 女士; nǚshì; Ms. / Madam Surname + 女士 (e.g., 李女士) 位 (wèi) 一位优雅的女士 (yí wèi yōuyǎ de nǚshì — an elegant lady) The safest, most respectful formal address for adult women regardless of marital status. Honorific / Gender HSK 1 小姐; xiǎojiě; Miss / Young lady Surname + 小姐 (e.g., 张小姐) 位 (wèi), 个 (gè) 两位买衣服的小姐 (liǎng wèi mǎi yīfu de xiǎojiě — two young ladies shopping) Standard in Taiwan/HK and with surnames; in mainland spoken Mandarin, avoid using it alone (prefer 美女 or 服务员). Honorific / Formal HSK 5 同志; tóngzhì; Comrade Title/Role + 同志 (e.g., 警察同志) 位 (wèi), 名 (míng) 一位热心的老同志 (yí wèi rèxīn de lǎo tóngzhì — a warm-hearted senior comrade) Traditional respectful address for public servants, officials, or older citizens; also modern slang for the LGBTQ+ community. Community / Kinship HSK 3 阿姨; āyí; Auntie Surname + 阿姨 / 阿姨 (e.g., 王阿姨) 位 (wèi), 个 (gè) 一个热情的保洁阿姨 (yí gè rèqíng de bǎojié āyí — a friendly cleaning auntie) Used for middle-aged/older women, friends' mothers, cleaners, and nannies. Community / Kinship HSK 3 叔叔; shūshu; Uncle Surname + 叔叔 / 叔叔 (e.g., 陈叔叔) 位 (wèi), 个 (gè) 一位热心的出租车叔叔 (yí wèi rèxīn de chūzūchē shūshu — an enthusiastic taxi uncle) Friendly address used by younger people toward men approximately their parents' age. Education HSK 1 老师; lǎoshī; Teacher / Mentor Surname + 老师 (e.g., 刘老师) 位 (wèi), 名 (míng) 一位负责任的老师 (yí wèi fù zérèn de lǎoshī — a responsible teacher) Broadly applied beyond schools to authors, artists, and respected mentors. Education HSK 5 教授; jiàoshòu; Professor Surname + 教授 (e.g., 张教授) 位 (wèi), 名 (míng) 一位著名的大学教授 (yí wèi zhùmíng de dàxué jiàoshòu — a renowned university professor) Prestigious academic title used in universities and research institutions. Education HSK 3 校长; xiàozhǎng; Principal / President Surname + 校长 (e.g., 李校长) 位 (wèi) 一位平易近人的校长 (yí wèi píngyì-jìnrén de xiàozhǎng — an approachable principal) Refers to both K-12 principals and university chancellors/presidents. Education HSK 1 同学; tóngxué; Classmate / Student Name + 同学 / 同学们 (e.g., 小王同学) 个 (gè), 名 (míng), 群 (qún) 三名新来的同学 (sān míng xīnlái de tóngxué — three newly arrived classmates) Used among peers, or by teachers addressing individual students. Healthcare HSK 1 / HSK 2 医生; yīshēng; Doctor / 大夫; dàifu; Physician Surname + 医生 / 大夫 (e.g., 赵医生 / 赵大夫) 位 (wèi), 名 (míng) 一位经验丰富的大夫 (yí wèi jīngyàn fēngfù de dàifu — an experienced physician) 大夫 (dàifu) is colloquial and especially popular in Northern China. Healthcare HSK 3 护士; hùshi; Nurse 护士 (Direct address) / 护士长 位 (wèi), 名 (míng), 个 (gè) 一名值夜班的护士 (yì míng zhí yèbān de hùshi — a nurse working the night shift) Addressed directly as 护士 or 护士小姐; head nurse is 护士长 (hùshizhǎng). Legal HSK 4 律师; lǜshī; Lawyer / Attorney Surname + 律师 (e.g., 孙律师) 位 (wèi), 名 (míng) 一位专业的辩护律师 (yí wèi zhuānyè de biànhù lǜshī — a professional defense attorney) Standard professional title inside and outside courtrooms. Trades & Blue-Collar HSK 4 师傅; shīfu; Master craftsman / Worker Surname + 师傅 / 师傅 (e.g., 司机师傅) 位 (wèi), 个 (gè) 一位修车的老师傅 (yí wèi xiūchē de lǎo shīfu — a veteran car repair master) Indispensable polite vocative for cab drivers, repairmen, tradespeople, and chefs. Service & Retail HSK 2 服务员; fúwùyuán; Attendant / Waiter 服务员！ (Direct call) 位 (wèi), 名 (míng), 个 (gè) 一个热情的餐厅服务员 (yí gè rèqíng de cāntīng fúwùyuán — an attentive restaurant waiter) The universal, polite call used in dining halls, hotels, and retail stores. Service & Retail HSK 4 售货员; shòuhuòyuán; Shop assistant / Clerk 售货员 / 你好 位 (wèi), 名 (míng), 个 (gè) 两名商场的售货员 (liǎng míng shāngchǎng de shòuhuòyuán — two mall sales clerks) Objective occupational title for department store and retail staff. Tourism & Sports HSK 4 导游; dǎoyóu; Tour guide Surname + 导 / 导游 (e.g., 王导) 位 (wèi), 名 (míng), 个 (gè) 一位负责任的地接导游 (yí wèi fù zérèn de dìjiē dǎoyóu — a responsible local tour guide) Tourists warmly call their guide [Surname] + 导 (e.g., 李导). Tourism & Sports HSK 5 教练; jiàoliàn; Coach / Trainer Surname + 教练 (e.g., 马教练) 位 (wèi), 名 (míng) 一位严厉的健身教练 (yí wèi yánlì de jiànshēn jiàoliàn — a strict fitness trainer) Used for driving instructors, gym personal trainers, and sports coaches. Public Services HSK 4 警察; jǐngchá; Police officer 警察同志 / 警察叔叔 位 (wèi), 名 (míng), 个 (gè) 两名巡逻的交警 (liǎng míng xúnluó de jiāojǐng — two patrolling traffic cops) 警察叔叔 is taught to children; 警察同志 is respectful for adults. Media HSK 4 记者; jìzhě; Journalist / Reporter Surname + 记者 (e.g., 陈记者) 位 (wèi), 名 (míng) 一名前往现场的记者 (yì míng qiánwǎng xiànchǎng de jìzhě — a reporter heading to the scene) Formal professional title used in broadcasts and press conferences. Workplace & Leadership HSK 5 老板; lǎobǎn; Boss / Proprietor Surname + 老板 / 老板 (e.g., 钱老板) 位 (wèi), 个 (gè) 一位白手起家的老板 (yí wèi báishǒu-qǐjiā de lǎobǎn — a self-made entrepreneur/boss) Standard address for business owners, startup founders, and small shopkeepers. Workplace & Leadership HSK 5 经理; jīnglǐ; Manager Surname + 经理 (e.g., 周经理) 位 (wèi), 名 (míng) 一位销售部门经理 (yí wèi xiàoshòu bùmén jīnglǐ — a sales department manager) Ubiquitous corporate title (总经理 = General Manager / CEO). Workplace & Leadership HSK 5 主任; zhǔrèn; Director / Dept Head Surname + 主任 (e.g., 吴主任) 位 (wèi), 名 (míng) 一位资深的主任医师 (yí wèi zīshēn de zhǔrèn yīshī — a senior chief physician) Common administrative title in hospitals, universities, and government bureaus. Workplace & Leadership HSK 5 领导; lǐngdǎo; Leader / Superior 领导 / 各位领导 位 (wèi) 一位重视团队的领导 (yí wèi zhòngshì tuánduì de lǐngdǎo — a leader who values teamwork) Used in workplaces to address bosses and senior executives diplomatically. Workplace & Peers HSK 3 同事; tóngshì; Colleague / Coworker Peer names / 同事们 个 (gè), 位 (wèi), 帮 (bāng) 一位配合默契的同事 (yí wèi pèihé mòqì de tóngshì — a coworker with great chemistry) Not used directly as a vocative prefix (use 老+Surname or 小+Surname instead). Events & High Status HSK 5 专家; zhuānjiā; Expert / Specialist 专家 / 专家老师 位 (wèi), 名 (míng) 一位国内顶尖的技术专家 (yí wèi guónèi dǐngjiān de jìshù zhuānjiā — a top domestic tech expert) Often paired respectfully as 专家老师 when addressing them in meetings. Events & High Status HSK 5 嘉宾; jiābīn; Honored guest / Panelist 各位嘉宾 (gèwèi jiābīn) 位 (wèi) 一位特邀出场的重量级嘉宾 (yí wèi tèyāo chūchǎng de zhòngliàngjí jiābīn — a special VIP guest) Standard term for VIPs, conference speakers, and banquet attendees.

💡 The Family Measure Word: 口; kǒu; Classifier for family members While 个; gè; General classifier is the general measure word, families are traditionally counted with 口; kǒu; Mouth (literally "mouth"), reflecting the number of mouths to feed around the dinner table. Context / Scenario Question Natural Response Example Ask Family Size 你家有几口人？; Nǐ jiā yǒu jǐ kǒu rén?; How many people are in your family? 我家有四口人：爸爸、妈妈、一个妹妹和我。; Wǒ jiā yǒu sì kǒu rén: bàba, māma, yí gè mèimei hé wǒ.; My family has 4: dad, mom, a younger sister, and me. Ask About Siblings 你有兄弟姐妹吗？; Nǐ yǒu xiōngdì jiěmèi ma?; Do you have any siblings? 我有一个哥哥，没有姐姐。; Wǒ yǒu yí gè gēge, méiyǒu jiějie.; I have an older br /other, but no older sisters. Introduce Someone 这位是谁？; Zhè wèi shì shéi?; Who is this? 这是我的同事，张先生。; Zhè shì wǒ de tóngshì, Zhāng xiānsheng.; This is my colleague, Mr. Zhang.
Counting in Mandarin is completely logical and mathematical. There are no irregular words like "eleven", "twelve", or "twenty"—every number is built from 0 to 10 like building blocks.
Digits 0 – 5 Digits 6 – 10 零; líng; 0 六; liù; 6 一; yī; 1 七; qī; 7 二; èr; 2 八; bā; 8 三; sān; 3 九; jiǔ; 9 四; sì; 4 十; shí; 10 五; wǔ; 5
You do not need to memorize any new vocabulary—simply add and multiply the core digits.

documents.t: Number Mathematical Breakdown 十一; shíyī; 11 10 + 1 十二; shí'èr; 12 10 + 2 十五; shíwǔ; 15 10 + 5 十九; shíjiǔ; 19 10 + 9
Number Mathematical Breakdown 二十; èrshí; 20 2 × 10 三十; sānshí; 30 3 × 10 八十; bāshí; 80 8 × 10
Number Mathematical Breakdown 二十一; èrshíyī; 21 (2 × 10) + 1 五十八; wǔshíbā; 58 (5 × 10) + 8 九十九; jiǔshíjiǔ; 99 (9 × 10) + 9
documents.s: C. Full Two-Digit Numbers ➔ [Tens Digit] × 十 + [Unit Digit]

documents.t: Before handling larger numbers, combine place values by stacking units from left to right: 百; bǎi; Hundred (100) 千; qiān; Thousand (1,000)

Number Usage & Notes 一百; yībǎi; 100 Must say yībǎi (never just bǎi alone) 二百; èrbǎi; 200 / 两百; liǎngbǎi; 200 Both forms are widely accepted 三百; sānbǎi; 300 3 × 100 一千; yīqiān; 1,000 1 × 1,000 两千; liǎngqiān; 2,000 两 (liǎng) is strongly preferred over 二 (èr)
Number Mathematical Breakdown 三百五十六; sānbǎi wǔshíliù; 356 300 + 50 + 6 七百八十九; qībǎi bāshíjiǔ; 789 700 + 80 + 9 两千四百六十八; liǎngqiān sìbǎi liùshíbā; 2,468 2,000 + 400 + 60 + 8

In English, place values change milestones every three zeroes (thousands ➔ millions ➔ billions). In Mandarin, place values change milestones every four zeroes (104): the primary milestone is 万 (wàn). 💡 The 4-Zero Mental Shortcut: Once you pass 9,999, mentally split the number by dropping the last 4 digits to find the number of 万 (wàn): 50,000 ➔ 5 + 0000 ➔ 五万 (wǔwàn) 350,000 ➔ 35 + 0000 ➔ 三十五万 (sānshíwǔwàn)

Number English Equivalent Mathematical Logic (Base 104) 一万; yīwàn; 10,000 10 Thousand 1 × 10,000 五万; wǔwàn; 50,000 50 Thousand 5 × 10,000 十万; shíwàn; 100,000 100 Thousand 10 × 10,000 一百万; yībǎiwàn; 1,000,000 1 Million 100 × 10,000 一千万; yīqiānwàn; 10,000,000 10 Million 1,000 × 10,000 一亿; yīyì; 100,000,000 100 Million New milestone tier (108)
Target Number Quick Mental Conversion 八万; bāwàn; 80,000 8 [0,000] ➔ 8 × 万 (wàn) 三十万; sānshíwàn; 300,000 30 [0,000] ➔ 30 × 万 (wàn) 五百万; wǔbǎiwàn; 5,000,000 500 [0,000] ➔ 500 × 万 (wàn)

Mandarin has two different words for the number 2. Using the correct one is crucial: 二; èr; 2 (digits/math): Used for counting digits, mathematics, dates, and codes. 两; liǎng; 2 (quantities): Used for quantities of physical things (placed before a measure word or time unit). Context Use 二 (èr) — Digits & Sequences Use 两 (liǎng) — Quantities Counting vs. Quantity 一二三; yī èr sān; 1, 2, 3 (sequence) 两个人; liǎng gè rén; Two people Names/Days vs. Objects 星期二; xīngqī'èr; Tuesday 两本书; liǎng běn shū; Two books Codes vs. Clock Time 房间 202; fángjiān èr-líng-èr; Room 202 两点钟; liǎng diǎn zhōng; 2 o'clock Tens vs. Thousands+ 二十二; èrshí'èr; 22 两千; liǎngqiān; 2,000
documents.s: Rule 1: The "Two" Battle — 二 (èr) vs. 两 (liǎng)

documents.t: Whenever there is an internal empty place value between non-zero digits, you must bridge the gap using 零; líng; 0: Number Breakdown Why 零 (líng) is Needed 一百零五; yībǎi líng wǔ; 105 100 + [0] + 5 Bridges the empty tens place 一千零八; yīqiān líng bā; 1,008 1,000 + [00] + 8 A single 零 bridges multiple consecutive empty slots 一万零五十; yīwàn líng wǔshí; 10,050 10,000 + [0] + 50 Bridges the empty hundreds slot

When reading out series of individual digits—such as phone numbers, room numbers, ID cards, and bus routes—the digit 一 (yī) is pronounced yāo: 💡 Why? Over a noisy phone line or radio, yī (1) sounds dangerously similar to qī (7). Pronouncing it as yāo guarantees zero confusion. Scenario Spoken Number Notes Hotel Room 108 一零八; yāo líng bā; 108 Hotel / apartment room number Emergency 110 一一零; yāo yāo líng; 110 Police emergency hotline / transit route Phone Number (138-1111) 138-1111; yāo sān bā, sì gè yāo Prevents mix-up with 7 (qī)
documents.s: Rule 3: The Phone & Code Rule, "一" Becomes Yāo (幺)

documents.t: Turning any cardinal counting number (1, 2, 3) into an ordinal rank (1st, 2nd, 3rd) requires zero irregular forms: simply add the prefix 第; dì; Prefix for ordinals (-th): Cardinal Base Ordinal Form (第 + #) 一; yī; 1 第一; dì-yī; 1st 二; èr; 2 第二; dì-'èr; 2nd 三; sān; 3 第三; dì-sān; 3rd 十; shí; 10 第十; dì-shí; 10th
In Mandarin, fractions and percentages are built around the concept of parts of a whole: 分之 (fēn zhī), which literally means "parts out of".

Unlike English, which states the top number (numerator) first ("three-quarters"), Mandarin always states the bottom number (denominator) first: Formula: Denominator + 分之 (fēn zhī) + Numerator (Literally: "Out of [Denominator] total parts, take [Numerator]") Fraction Literal Breakdown 二分之一; èrfēnzhīyī; 1/2 (One half) Out of 2 parts, 1 (or simply 半; bàn; Half) 三分之一; sānfēnzhīyī; 1/3 (One third) Out of 3 parts, 1 四分之三; sìfēnzhīsān; 3/4 (Three-fourths) Out of 4 parts, 3 五分之二; wǔfēnzhī'èr; 2/5 (Two-fifths) Out of 5 parts, 2

Percentages are simply fractions out of 100 ("Out of 100 parts, take X"): Percentage Literal Breakdown 百分之一; bǎifēnzhīyī; 1% Out of 100 parts, 1 百分之五十; bǎifēnzhī wǔshí; 50% Out of 100 parts, 50 百分之百; bǎifēnzhī bǎi; 100% Out of 100 parts, 100 (completely)

⚠️ The Big Cultural Inversion: In Western stores, a tag saying "20% OFF" tells you what you save. In China, store discounts tell you what percentage of the original price you pay: Discount Term Meaning 九折; jiǔ zhé; 10% OFF Pay 90% of original price 八折; bā zhé; 20% OFF Pay 80% of original price 七五折; qīwǔ zhé; 25% OFF Pay 75% of original price 五折; wǔ zhé; 50% OFF Pay 50% of original price (Half price)
documents.s: C. The Chinese Discount Trap: 打折 (dǎzhé)

documents.t: The decimal point is pronounced 点; diǎn; Point / Dot (literally "dot" or "point"). 💡 The Reading Rule: Read the numbers before the decimal point as a standard whole number. Read the numbers after the decimal point as individual single digits. Decimal Breakdown 零点五; líng diǎn wǔ; 0.5 Zero + dot + five 三点一四; sān diǎn yī sì; 3.14 (Pi) Three + dot + one + four 二十八点六五; èrshíbā diǎn liù wǔ; 28.65 Twenty-eight + dot + six + five 百分之零点零一; bǎifēnzhī líng diǎn líng yī; 0.01% Out of 100 + zero + dot + zero + one
In Chinese culture, numbers carry immense symbolic weight due to homophones—words that sound nearly identical to fortunate or unfortunate words.

Number Sounds Like (Homophone) Cultural Meaning & Real-World Impact 八; bā; 8 发; fā; To prosper / get rich The Luckiest Number: License plates, phone numbers, and apartment floors with "8" sell for massive premiums. The Beijing Olympics opened on 08/08/08 at 8:08 PM. 六; liù; 6 流; liú; Flow Good Fortune & Success: Associated with things moving smoothly without obstacles (六六大顺; liùliù dàshùn; Everything goes smoothly). Also used as internet slang (666) for "awesome" or "pro". 九; jiǔ; 9 久; jiǔ; Long-lasting / Eternal Eternity & Royalty: Historically reserved for the Emperor (9 dragons, 9,999 rooms in the Forbidden City). Common in romantic contexts (e.g., gifting 99 roses). 四; sì; 4 死; sǐ; Death The Ultimate Taboo (Tetraphobia): Differing only by tone, "4" is strictly avoided. Many hospitals, hotels, and high-rise residential buildings in China completely skip the 4th, 14th, and 24th floors.

Young Chinese netizens frequently use sequences of digits as phonetic shortcuts in text messaging: Number Code Sounds Like Usage Context 520 (wǔ-èr-líng) 我爱你; wǒ ài nǐ; I love you May 20th (5/20) is celebrated as China's modern digital Valentine's Day. 1314 (yī-sān-yī-sì) 一生一世; yīshēng yīshì; One life, one lifetime Represents eternal love; frequently paired as 5201314 ("I love you for a lifetime"). 250 (èr-bǎi-wǔ) (Fool / Idiot) Derived from ancient currency strings; calling someone an èrbǎiwǔ means they are a blockhead. 555 (wǔ-wǔ-wǔ) 呜呜呜; wūwūwū; Crying sound (waaah) Used in chat to express sadness, crying, or mock weeping.

note Telling time in Mandarin follows a strictly logical Largest Unit ➔ Smallest Unit hierarchy: Part of Day (AM/PM) ➔ 点; diǎn; O'clock ➔ 分; fēn; Minute (e.g., "Afternoon ➔ 3 o'clock ➔ 15 minutes") 分钟 (fēnzhōng) refers strictly to duration (how long an event lasts). Example: 我等了三分钟。(Wǒ děng le sān fēnzhōng.) — "I waited for three minutes." Example: 请给我五分钟。(Qǐng gěi wǒ wǔ fēnzhōng.) — "Please give me five minutes."

Concept Formula Example Sentence Asking the Time — 现在几点了？; Xiànzài jǐ diǎn le?; What time is it now? Standard Time [Hr] + 点 + [Min] + 分 三点十分; sān diǎn shí fēn; 3:10 On the Hour [Hr] + 点 + (整) 三点整; sān diǎn zhěng; 3:00 sharp Minutes To 差 + [Min] + 分 + [Next Hr] + 点 差十分八点; chà shí fēn bā diǎn; 7:50 (10 to 8)

Rule Description Incorrect ❌ Correct ✅ Why? 1. The "Two" Rule Use 两; liǎng; Two (quantity), never 二; èr; Two (digit) for 2 o'clock. 二点 (èr diǎn) 两点; liǎng diǎn; 2 o'clock Clock hours are a measured quantity. 2. The "Zero" Rule For minutes 01–09, you must say 零; líng; 0. 四点五分 (sì diǎn wǔ fēn) 四点零五分; sì diǎn líng wǔ fēn; 4:05 Fills the empty tens place (4:05). 3. Dropping 分 (fēn) When minutes are two digits (10–59), drop 分; fēn; Minute. — 八点二十; bā diǎn èrshí; 8:20 Dropping fēn sounds natural and fluent (8:20).

Native speakers rely on three common shortcuts rather than counting individual minutes: Shortcut Pattern / Unit Example :15 (Quarter past) 一刻; yí kè; 1 quarter (15 min) 九点一刻; jiǔ diǎn yí kè; 9:15 (quarter past 9) :30 (Half past) 半; bàn; Half (30 min) 四点半; sì diǎn bàn; 4:30 (half past 4) :45 (Quarter to) 差一刻; chà yí kè; Quarter to 差一刻十点; chà yí kè shí diǎn; 9:45 (quarter to 10) (Note: While 三刻; sān kè; 3 quarters (:45) exists for :45, 差一刻; chà yí kè; Quarter to is much more common in daily speech).

documents.t: Chinese does not use abbreviations like "AM" or "PM". Instead, specify the period of the day before the hour: Order: Period of Day ➔ [Hour] + 点; diǎn; O'clock ➔ [Minute] + 分; fēn; Minute Time Range Period of Day Example 1:00 AM – 5:59 AM 凌晨; língchén; Early morning 凌晨三点; língchén sān diǎn; 3:00 AM 6:00 AM – 8:59 AM 早上; zǎoshang; Morning 早上八点; zǎoshang bā diǎn; 8:00 AM 9:00 AM – 11:59 AM 上午; shàngwǔ; Late morning 上午十点半; shàngwǔ shí diǎn bàn; 10:30 AM 12:00 PM – 12:59 PM 中午; zhōngwǔ; Noon 中午十二点; zhōngwǔ shí'èr diǎn; 12:00 PM 1:00 PM – 5:59 PM 下午; xiàwǔ; Afternoon 下午三点一刻; xiàwǔ sān diǎn yí kè; 3:15 PM 6:00 PM onwards 晚上; wǎnshang; Evening / Night 晚上九点; wǎnshang jiǔ diǎn; 9:00 PM
documents.s: 4. Periods of the Day (AM vs. PM in Chinese)

documents.t: ⚠️ The Golden Word Order Rule: In English, time usually sits at the end of a sentence ("I eat lunch at 12:00"). In Mandarin, time MUST go BEFORE the verb: Activity Example Sentence Literal Word Order Wake Up 我早上七点起床。; Wǒ zǎoshang qī diǎn qǐchuáng.; I wake up at 7:00 AM. I + morning 7:00 + wake up Eat Lunch 我们中午十二点吃午饭。; Wǒmen zhōngwǔ shí'èr diǎn chī wǔfàn.; We eat lunch at 12:00 PM. We + noon 12:00 + eat lunch Finish Work 他下午六点下班。; Tā xiàwǔ liù diǎn xiàbān.; He finishes work at 6:00 PM. He + afternoon 6:00 + finish work Go to Sleep 我晚上十一点半睡觉。; Wǒ wǎnshang shíyī diǎn bàn shuìjiào.; I go to sleep at 11:30 PM. I + night 11:30 + go to sleep
